transcript.text: While tracing a separate permissions bug yesterday, I found that 23 legacy admin endpoints update permissions without emitting the invalidation event consumed by the new cache. I haven't filed the adapter work yet because I was confirming which endpoints still use that path. The rollout plan must include a binding commitment to build and verify an invalidation adapter for those 23 endpoints before expanding beyond the initial cohort.

transcript.text: My load rehearsal this morning measured invalidation-queue propagation at a 9-minute p95 and showed that the queue stays within its safe operating limit only when the first rollout cohort is capped at 10 percent. Also, for this rollout the authorization cache lifetime must be set to exactly 300 seconds. I haven't updated the rollout ticket yet because the rehearsal finished after the change-control review began.

transcript.text: During a support-case review, I confirmed that all 11 SCIM-managed enterprise accounts use an admin workflow that cannot yet explain delayed permission changes. Those accounts must be excluded from the first rollout, and a support playbook must be prepared before they are enabled. I hadn't posted this yet because the cases were being reassigned between support queues.

transcript.text:
Thank you all for surfacing these findings before I finalize the flag settings. Let me confirm what I'm hearing and how I plan to incorporate each constraint:

1. Mina — 23 legacy admin endpoints silently update permissions without emitting the invalidation event the new cache depends on. I'll treat the invalidation adapter for those endpoints as a binding prerequisite before we expand beyond the initial cohort.

2. Owen — Load rehearsal shows a 9-minute p95 on invalidation-queue propagation, and the queue stays within safe limits only if the first cohort is capped at 10%. Cache TTL must be exactly 300 seconds. I'll set both accordingly.

3. Tessa — All 11 SCIM-managed enterprise accounts use an admin workflow that can't handle delayed permission changes yet. Those accounts must be excluded from the first rollout, and a support playbook must be ready before they're ever enabled.

Based on all three findings, here's the rollout policy I'm preparing to settle:
- Initial rollout: 10% of traffic (non-SCIM enterprise accounts only)
- Cache TTL: exactly 300 seconds
- Excluded segment: SCIM-managed enterprise accounts
- Binding commitment: build and verify the invalidation adapter for the 23 legacy endpoints before expanding beyond the initial cohort
- Binding commitment: prepare a support playbook for SCIM-managed accounts before enabling them
- Revocation kill switch: enabled, so we can immediately disable the flag if we observe stale-permission issues in production

Does anyone have additional operational constraints I should factor in before I finalize?
